questions.title: Why does the Federal Circuit apply Fifth Circuit law when reviewing a district court's denial of JMOL in a patent appeal?
questions.question_body: In *Finesse Wireless LLC v. AT&T Mobility LLC* the opinion states that "we review a district court's denial of JMOL under the law of the regional circuit, here the Fifth Circuit." I thought appeals from district courts on patent matters automatically fell under Federal Circuit precedent for standards like de novo review of claim construction and substantial‑evidence review for factual findings. Is there a statutory or procedural reason why the Court adopts the Fifth Circuit's approach here? Does 28 U.S.C. §1295(a)(1) require borrowing regional circuit law for certain issues, or is this discretionary?

questions.title: Does amending patent claims from "two or three signals" to "three signals" constitute a clear‑and‑unambiguous disavowal of two‑signal implementations?
questions.question_body: The '775 patent originally described "digitally multiplying two or three signals" during prosecution, but Finesse amended the claims to require "three signals S1, S2 and S3." The Federal Circuit held that this amendment did not rise to a "clear and unambiguous" disavowal of coverage for radios that use only two unique input signals. I'm trying to understand what level of specificity in an amendment triggers forfeiture of claim scope. What factors do courts consider when deciding whether an amendment disavows certain embodiments? Are there leading cases that define how explicit an amendment must be to surrender coverage over two‑signal devices?

questions.title: How should "separately identifiable" be interpreted in patent claims that do not require unique input signals?
questions.question_body: In construing claim 1 of the '775 patent, the district court held that "three signals S1, S2 and S3" must be "separately identifiable" but not necessarily unique, relying on inventor testimony that these signals can be the same waveform or different ones. On appeal this interpretation was upheld. Does "separately identifiable" merely mean that the claimant can label three instances differently even if they are physically identical? What case law explains whether identical signals satisfy a requirement for separate identifiability?

questions.title: When an expert's testimony contains self‑contradictions about mapping claim elements to device components, can a jury's infringement verdict survive under the substantial‑evidence standard?
questions.question_body: Dr. Wells' expert testimony in *Finesse* was inconsistent: at times he said x1 and x2 mapped onto "signals of interest" and "interference generating signals," while elsewhere he relied on labels like DL(TX) reference and modeled PIM path without clearly linking them to those claim elements. The Federal Circuit concluded these contradictions meant there was no substantial evidence supporting infringement. How do courts evaluate such contradictory expert statements? Is any inconsistency fatal, or must it rise to a particular level before overturning a jury finding? What authorities guide this analysis?

questions.title: What weight can extrinsic evidence such as inventor testimony carry in claim construction when intrinsic record is ambiguous?
questions.question_body: For the '775 patent claims, the district court gave considerable weight to inventor testimony stating that S1‑S3 could represent either distinct or identical signals, despite ambiguous intrinsic language in the specification. The appellate court affirmed this approach. I'm unclear about how courts balance intrinsic versus extrinsic evidence in claim construction decisions. Under what circumstances can inventor or other extrinsic statements outweigh unclear written description? Are there Supreme Court or Federal Circuit precedents that delineate this hierarchy?

questions.title: Why does reversing every asserted claim of infringement automatically vacate a jury's damages award rather than remanding for further damage determination?
questions.question_body: *Finesse* had a $166 million lump‑sum verdict based on infringement findings across all asserted claims. After reversing both denials of JMOL for noninfringement on every asserted claim, the Federal Circuit vacated the entire damages award without ordering a remand on damages alone. Is it standard practice that if infringement is found lacking on all claimed patents then any damage award must be vacated entirely? Could there be scenarios where some claims survive and only part of an award is adjusted? Which authorities govern vacating versus remanding damages after an infringement reversal?
